column51: 2/10ths cloud cover. 19 deg C.   We walked part way up one bank of the river, waded across into a plantation on the North Side and followed it upstream and eventually into San Jose del Cabo. Lunched there.   Picked up a different trail on the way back to the beach.  A November rainstorm and flood produced massive and disasterous damage here.  There were riverside houses with debris and hard baked mud upto the top of first floor windows, 7 metres higher than today's water levels. Foundations undermined, none of them look repairable.  On the beachfront there are two hotels closed and their pools filled with mud and debris.

In March 23 and April 3, 2000, I participated in a West Virginia University Field Ornithology class that traveled through the Baja Peninsula. The class was led by Dr. Robert C. Whitmore, Division of Forestry, Wildlife and Fisheries Science and Management. We arrived at 1:40 PM in Cabos San Lucas and traveled to Centro de Investigaciones Biológicas del Noroeste among other locations. Dr. Whitmore was studying Brown thrashers and Yellow "Mangrove" warblers, in particular. These records are recorded from a detailed field notebook that included maps, sketches, descriptions, and other notes. There were approximately 10 to 12 students on this trip and although we observed species as a group, we oftentimes were dispersed in groups of two. Mist-netting and song playback were used at some locations. Temperature and weather were mid 80s and breezy, cooling into late afternoon and evening. This was a memorable trip and contributed toward my curiosity and admiration of desert ecosystems, rural lifestyles, and global surf culture. The people were kind and interesting. The food was fantastic. The heat was real. The desert and coast were magnificent. Oh yes... and the birds!

column52: The sub-adult or first summer YELLOW-CROWNED NIGHT-HERON has been around here since about 20 June. We got very good looks at it and I took several photos. The most notable field marks separating it from Black-crowned Night-Heron were the very stout, thick shorter bill, longer legs and neck, and the beginnings of an adult face pattern. The bird was overall somewhat mottled gray with a bright orange eye. There was a distinctive cream colored crown stripe and a cream colored stripe under the eye starting at the base of the bill and extending beyond the eye. The wing coverts were gray with black centers. The legs were black or dark on the front and yellowish on the back. The breast had several streaks of the same cream color.

I got a good view of the yellow-crowned night heron''s face and back when it was in flight.  On the face, I clearly saw a line of black under the line of white, which was under a line of black.  The back was all the same shade of gray, unlike the two-color pattern on black-crowned.  I talked to someone at the visitor center who verified that indeed there have been a pair of yellow-crowned night-herons nesting in a local apartment building (where I saw the bird flying to), for the third consecutive year.  I also heard a bird in the distance, out in the marsh, that was making a weird upslurred sound, un-duck-like but with the tone quality of a duck.  It was not a sound I recognized.  I heard 3 clapper rails (at least), but I only was able to get a glimpse maybe of 1, although the view was not good enough to ID it.  I also noted that one of the western gulls was moulting.
These observations were made on the Birding Along the Border Trip, which was part of the 2008 San Diego Bird Festival.  I can provide a photo of the Yellow-crowned Night-Heron if necessary.

reported by Robert McMorran then re-found by Oscar Johnson just before I ran into him at about 2:50pm.  Ourselves and Carol & Bob Langford viewed this bird from the RR trestle after it had flushed into the Ventura River mouth esturary.

I chased this bird at the estuary and found it quite easily. It was not seen subsequently. I neglected to keep an ebird checklist though... Date recovered from the CBRC record. Accepted record 2008-056.----CBRC report: --Species: Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, Nyctanassa violacea--Location: Ventura River Mouth, Ventura County.--Date: 13 April 2008--Age and sex: After hatch year, sex unknown--Molt status: None apparent--Number of individuals: 1--Other observers: Eric Waian, two other people I didn’t know--Original observers: Robert and Allison McMorran------Circumstances: I got a message from Robert in the midafternoon of the 13th, after spending all morning hiking, so I raced down to Ventura. Once I got to the Ventura River Mouth I walked out to the river from the Emma Wood State Beach campground, and started walking along the overgrown gravel bar towards the railroad bridge and the river mouth. I didn’t make it 200 feet before a mid-sized dark heron flushed from some reeds along the shore about forty feet in front of me and flew behind me in good light at about twenty foot elevation and headed out to the sand bars at the river mouth. I recognized it as the Yellow-crowned and headed back onto the trails through the willows to get out to the railroad bridge so that I would have a better view of the bird. I ran into Eric on the trails, who hadn’t seen the bird yet, so we both headed out to the bridge, where there were other two birders looking in the wrong direction. The heron was easily visible and we all got good looks through the scope (although a little distant) and I got some decent digiscoped photos. After watching the bird for about fifteen-twenty minutes, I had to leave to return to Santa Barbara. ----Description: A mid-sized dark gray heron, approximately the same size as a Black-crowned Night-Heron (although there were none for direct comparison). The neck and legs were rather short for a heron. In flight the grayish legs extended slightly beyond the short tail. When perched, the tail was mostly hidden by the wings, which were plain gray and slightly darker than the rest of the body. The head was black, fading into the gray of the neck. The crown was white, broad towards the bill, and becoming narrow towards the nape. Another white blaze started just bellow the eye as a narrow point, and became wider as it curved slightly up towards the nape. The bill was very stocky, with a curved culmen, and dark grey. I did not note the eye color.----Discussion: A very distinctive heron. Much smaller than Great Blue, and much larger than Green, the two expected dark herons in the area. Tricolored Heron has a white belly, and Reddish Egret and Little Blue Heron are solidly dark, including on the head. Black-crowned Night-Heron is much paler, and has a black crown, among other characters.

column52: This bird had been found by Wes Fritz on 29 January 2010, and was seen by many observers over the next couple of weeks. I saw the bird the first day, but did not write up my observations due to an illness that struck me the next day. I returned to see the bird on 13 February, when I found it in the same area where I had seen it previously, in willows visible from a foot bridge leading across the creek to the Bacara Resort. The bird remained on the same branch, stationary, the entire time I was present. I watched it for 10 or 15 minutes, recorded my observations on my iPhone, and transcribed this description from those observations a month later. ----Description: A small, pale buffy area on the chin, but otherwise very gray below, wrapping around the auriculars, which were black surrounding a whitish area in the center. The crown was gray from the top of the bill backward to about mid-crown and appeared black from the center backward. My notes mentioned adult-like white plumes, but don¿t say anything about length of placement of the plumes. A brownish area could be seen adjacent to the bend in the wing. The wing coverts were gray and brown, with buffy edging to all of the these feathers, which also had dark feather shafts. The flight feathers weren¿t clearly visible; it did appear that they were dark, but it wasn¿t evident whether or not they had pale edges. I couldn¿t see the mantle and tail well.----The bill was mostly blackish or dark gray, but with a yellow area on the mandible concentrated at the base. It was longer than that of Black-crowned Night-Heron, and the culmen was more curved, giving the bill a slightly droopy look. The legs were also long compared to those of Black-crowned Night-Herons. The bird kept its eyes closed most of the time I watched it. The eyelid was gray, and the eye was dark orangish red.

Accepted by CBRC. Description: A mid-sized heron, approximately the same size as the nearby 5 or so Black-crowned Night-Herons. The body size was possibly a little bit slimmer than that species though. The bill was mostly black with a small amount of green near the base, and slightly shorter and stouter than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron. The body plumage was almost entirely even slate-gray, with a slight wash of brown to some portions. The wing coverts and mantle feathers were all lanceolate in shape, each with a thin gray-brown border and a dark gray center. The tail was short and looked to be dark, but I did not take much note of it. The neck was short and the head was held close to the body, thus further accentuating the shortness of the neck. The throat and malar area were black, extending back to the lower nape to connect with very broad black supercilium. This area of black surrounded a broad whitish line that extended back from the eye through the auricular. The crown stripe was grayish-white, contrasting relatively little with the broad black supercilium. There were two short thin white plumes extending from the rear of the crown, and a small spot of white barely visible on the chin. The legs were lime green, and the eye was dark red.

column52: One immature confirmed dead and et, 2nd looking good

I looked at these birds only briefly, yet I was clearly able to note most of the key characters.  The bird that I saw best was a medium-sized heron with a stocky body, a large and somewhat blocky head that had a somewhat flat-crowned appearance, and a conspicuously large and noticeably massive bill.  The forehead and crown were creamy-yellow to whitish, and there was a complementary stripe across the auriculars that was again creamy, if not white.  The rest of the head was blackish, if not truly black, apparently including the supraloral and superciliary regions, and the lower part of the face below the white stripe.  What was visible of the body and underparts was instead a clear gray in coloration.  The underparts appeared to be unmarked, but the wings were boldly marked with what appeared to be pale gray fringes on the coverts that produced a pattern of fine streaking or possibly scaling, and fine striping of pale gray on the remiges along the leading edge of the wing.  I never did see this bird's back or tail. column51: Left work for the Yellow-crowned Night-Heron in the Pocket Marsh between the Bolsa Chica Mesa and the Wintersburg Channel. This area of muted tidal flow has been good for BCNHs that forage and roost among the dead eucalyptus trees that line the western and northern margins of this restored salt marsh habitat (dead eucalyptus are a result of allowing tidal flushing in this area). I parked at the end of Bolsa Chica Street at the same time as Jon Dunn and Larry Sansone. Brian Leatherman was just leaving and said the bird was still there and that Leo Ohtsuki was looking at it. We took the Brightwater Trail down to the north end of the “pocket” marsh and followed the unmarked trail along the west side of the Pocket Marsh until we found Leo and Jim Roe – the bird was less than 50 feet away sitting by itself on a dead eucalyptus lying on the water. Other birders arrived while I was there including Curtis Marantz.
column52: A juvenile with brownish gray plumage marked with small white spots and edges. The underparts were whitish with dark brown streaks. The bill was heavy and black (it did show some yellowish at base of lower mandible but none along the cutting edge of the bill). The legs were pale and appeared relatively long (there was no adjacent Black-crowned Night-Heron for direct comparison – they were nearby but when I looked at them for comparison, I only considered the bill shape and covert pattern and forgot about leg length). The coverts had neat white fringes and a smallish white triangular shaped white spot at tip of feather. The primaries were tipped thinly with white. The back was dark grayish brown (overall the feathers looked worn, but some of the mantle feathers were darker and may have been fresh indicating second generation of feathers). The scapulars as well as the head had smaller and more elongated versions of this triangular shaped white spots. A white streak below the eye was evident (Joe Morlan mentioned this on his Monday post to Orange County Birding as possibly a mark for YCNH). The eye color (iris) was orangish and the unfeathered lores were yellowish.

Given that Guy knew precisely where to look, we managed to see three of the adult birds in association with two different nests, one in a large pine and another in a broad-leaf ornamental over the parking lot.  I was able to note among these birds the large size, stocky body, blocky head with a somewhat flat-crowned appearance, and a rather massive bill that tapered from a heavy base to a pointed tip.  I think I saw all three birds well enough to see the clean-gray body and, on at least one of these birds, I saw clearly the paler gray fringes on the coverts and remiges that created both a scaly pattern to the upper part of the wings and a striped pattern to the lower part.  On at least two of these birds I was able to make out the bold pattern on the head that combined a yellowish forehead and crown, the mostly black sides of the head, and a whitish stripe across the face that began narrowly below the eye before broadening as it extended across the auriculars.  I used my 10 × 42 binoculars to study these birds, which we saw under the muted light that resulted from the overcast skies.  Given that I have seen these birds repeatedly over the course of the last several years, I did not study them all that carefully and I then waited several weeks to write a description, so my recollection of these birds is a bit fuzzier, and thus my description somewhat more superficial, than usual.  I can say confidently, however, that we saw all three birds well enough to identify them unequivocally as adult Yellow-crowned Night-Herons.

It took some effort, but Dick eventually spotted one of the nesting pairs of Yellow-crowned Night-Herons in a densely vegetated pine along the western fence line of the park.  I studied these birds only briefly before we continued on our way, and we never did locate the second nesting pair.  One bird was sitting on a nest and the other was perched less than a meter away on a nearby branch.  We never heard these birds, which remained essentially motionless during our visit and, in general, with one of the birds facing away from us.  Both birds were plump herons of medium size with short wings and tails.  The bird on the nest had the typical, massive bill of this species that tapered from a heavy base to a bluntly pointed tip along a slightly decurved culmen, but I was unable to see this bird's legs.  The second bird was facing away, so it was difficult to see much of the bill, though what I did see was similar to that of the bird on the nest.  This bird also had medium-length legs that were relatively stout.--Both birds were a medium-gray color overall, but they had a boldly striped appearance that resulted from well-defined fringes of whitish to pale yellow on the wing coverts and remiges.  I think I saw the underparts only on the bird on the nest and what I saw appeared to be gray an unmarked.  I noted on the bird on the nest that the forehead and crown were creamy-yellow with the forehead somewhat more deeply colored, and that there was a complementary band of pale yellow to creamy-whitish that extended across the lower part of the face, but the head was otherwise blackish.  On the perched bird, I noted only an indication of the yellow forehead, pale facial stripe, and generally black head, but my views of this bird's head were not very good.  The bird seen best appeared to have an entirely black bill and, as I recall, reddish eyes, but I cannot now recall seeing the soft-part colored in any more detail.

column52: I spotted first one and then two more adult birds perched in the pines over the parking lot in the apartment complex immediately west of the park.  We were then invited by one of the residents to observe these birds from the complex, and once here, we discovered that one of the birds was standing in the open in good light.  Having seen these birds so many times over the last few years, I did not study them all that carefully, yet I saw each of the three more than well enough to make a definitive identification.  These were medium-sized herons with large and somewhat blocky heads, massive bills, retracted necks, and plump bodies with an upright posture, short wings, and even shorter tails.  I must admit that my views were restricted to the head, neck, and underparts on two of these birds, but the one we photographed was standing fully in the open.  It was only on this bird that I saw the moderately long, stout legs.--All three birds had blackish heads with the forehead and crown pale, and a whitish stripe that extended from just below the eye back across the auriculars.  I also noted on the bird we saw best a long, filamentous plume extending back and down from the crown.  The neck and underparts were medium-gray and unmarked, but the back and wings were a somewhat darker shade of gray with well-defined edges of light gray that created a boldly striped pattern to at least the wing coverts and remiges.  I cannot now recall if I ever saw a primary projection, and I am pretty sure I never clearly saw the tail.  The bill was entirely black and the legs were yellowish, but I cannot now recall the color of the eyes.  I noted a similar pattern on the head of the other two birds, and that both had unmarked, gray underparts, but I cannot recall seeing the upperparts well on these birds as they roosted in locations that were harder to see clearly.----<iframe src="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/12315952824/player/0b60b270c5" height="533" width="800" frameborder="0"></iframe>

column52: Juvenile, present several days. Blackish crown with pin feathers present. Greater, median, and lesser coverts dark with small, well-defined, triangular white spots at tips. Fine pale brownish-buff edges to greater coverts, flight feathers very dark gray, as appears on folded wing. Outer primaries with very fine brownish buff edges. Breast and belly brownish gray with fine, distinct pale streaks. Under tail coverts whitish. Bill thick compared to Black-crowned Night-Heron, with distinct curvature of both maxilla and mandible forming symmetrical shape. Bill dark gray with some pale, yellowish white along mandible. Eye reddish orange, darker than expected of BCNH. Some photos of this bird have shown a yellow bare area above the lores, but I can't see this in my view (well lit from 25 feet). In comparison with nearby juvenile BCNH, lacks brownish tones on greater coverts and flight feathers, extensively greenish lores, elongated spots on tips of coverts, extensive pale on mandible extending into maxilla. Also BCNH appears shorter legged and lacks narrow edges to greater coverts. Watched the bird perched at this distance at my leisure for extended period.--<iframe src="https://www.flickr.com/photos/15019258@N02/15209765846/in/photostream/player/" width="500" height="359" frameborder="0"></iframe>

column52: **First record for the Carpinteria Salt Marsh, third Santa Barbara County record. Juvenile bird first seen along the edge of Franklin Creek near the entrance to Sandyland, standing in the shade under overhanging salacornia plants. This portion of the marsh is private property, and we obtained permission in advance to access this area. The bird initially appeared dark with limited white spotting and the bill appeared large and mostly dark. Closer inspection with a spotting scope revealed small white spots on the wing coverts, a heavily streaked breast and face, and a large yellow-orange eye. The angle of the forehead from the base of the bill was relatively steep. column52: Continuing second year bird initially found by Matt Gearheart on 23 Sep, and seen again by Guy McCaskie on 25 Sep. While scanning the area where Guy had reported seeing it, I (TAB) noticed a large grayish blob standing in the water within a patch of dry reeds, and I was able to see enough of the head pattern to determine that it was the YCNH. We were able to obtain scope views of the bird, but it was largely obscured by the reeds. After ten or fifteen minutes of these obstructed views, the bird miraculously flew out of the reeds and landed on some matted-down reeds along the east edge of the same pond, allowing unobstructed views for another ten minutes. This was a small, rather stocky heron with long legs (the tail extending to a point just below the ankles while standing, and the tarsi and feet extending well beyond the tail tip in flight). Over all the bird was primarily dark gray. The feathers of the upper parts were dark gray with pale gray edges, creating a neatly scalloped appearance. The under parts were also mostly gray, but with some whitish streaking throughout indicative of retained juvenile plumage. The head pattern was diagnostic, being blackish with a narrow, creamy-white stripe extending from the gape of the bill underneath the eye and widening to its terminus at the nape, and a grayish-yellow forehead that extended posteriorly and became narrower over the crown to its terminus at the nape. The iris was a striking red-orange color, and there was a single white filoplume extending from the hindcrown. The bill was primarily blackish, and noticeably "heavy" and deep. Matt Grube's flight photos showed a mixture of contrasting new and retained remiges, also indicative of a second year bird.

column52: I spotted first one and then two more adult birds perched in the pines over the parking lot in the apartment complex immediately west of the park.  We were then invited by one of the residents to observe these birds from the complex, and once here, we discovered that one of the birds was standing in the open in good light.  Having seen these birds so many times over the last few years, I did not study them all that carefully, yet I saw each of the three more than well enough to make a definitive identification.  These were medium-sized herons with large and somewhat blocky heads, massive bills, retracted necks, and plump bodies with an upright posture, short wings, and even shorter tails.  I must admit that my views were restricted to the head, neck, and underparts on two of these birds, but the one we photographed was standing fully in the open.  It was only on this bird that I saw the moderately long, stout legs.--All three birds had blackish heads with the forehead and crown pale, and a whitish stripe that extended from just below the eye back across the auriculars.  I also noted on the bird we saw best a long, filamentous plume extending back and down from the crown.  The neck and underparts were medium-gray and unmarked, but the back and wings were a somewhat darker shade of gray with well-defined edges of light gray that created a boldly striped pattern to at least the wing coverts and remiges.  I cannot now recall if I ever saw a primary projection, and I am pretty sure I never clearly saw the tail.  The bill was entirely black and the legs were yellowish, but I cannot now recall the color of the eyes.  I noted a similar pattern on the head of the other two birds, and that both had unmarked, gray underparts, but I cannot recall seeing the upperparts well on these birds as they roosted in locations that were harder to see clearly.----<iframe src="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/12315952824/player/0b60b270c5" height="533" width="800" frameborder="0"></iframe>

While scanning the area where Guy had reported seeing it, I (TAB) noticed a large grayish blob standing in the water within a patch of dry reeds, and I was able to see enough of the head pattern to determine that it was the YCNH. We were able to obtain scope views of the bird, but it was largely obscured by the reeds. After ten or fifteen minutes of these obstructed views, the bird miraculously flew out of the reeds and landed on some matted-down reeds along the east edge of the same pond, allowing unobstructed views for another ten minutes. This was a small, rather stocky heron with long legs (the tail extending to a point just below the ankles while standing, and the tarsi and feet extending well beyond the tail tip in flight). Over all the bird was primarily dark gray. The feathers of the upper parts were dark gray with pale gray edges, creating a neatly scalloped appearance. The under parts were also mostly gray, but with some whitish streaking throughout indicative of retained juvenile plumage. The head pattern was diagnostic, being blackish with a narrow, creamy-white stripe extending from the gape of the bill underneath the eye and widening to its terminus at the nape, and a grayish-yellow forehead that extended posteriorly and became narrower over the crown to its terminus at the nape. The iris was a striking red-orange color, and there was a single white filoplume extending from the hindcrown. The bill was primarily blackish, and noticeably "heavy" and deep. Matt Grube's flight photos showed a mixture of contrasting new and retained remiges, also indicative of a second year bird.

column52: Shortly after we began our search for the resident night-herons Paul located three birds roosting in a broadleaf tree at the edge of the parking lot near the restrooms.  As I recall, this is one of the trees in which these birds have nested in past seasons.  The adult was standing near a nest, but I am not sure these birds have begun preparing their nest for the up[conign season.  The two young birds were perched singly not too far away, but also in the upper branches of the trees amid the moderately dense vegetation.  The angle was less than ideal for observing these birds from below, yet we were able to see more than enough to identify them and I even took a few photos.--All three birds were stocky herons with rather massive bills, blocky heads with what appeared a steep forehead and a somewhat flattened crown, at least on the adult, which I saw best.  All three birds had the neck retracted, and all three had a plump body, a full-chested appearance, and an upright posture.  The wings and tail both appeared to be relatively short, btu the legs were long and stout.--The adult bird had a blackish head with a butter-yellow forehead, but I could not clearly see the crown and I cannot now recall even seeing the pale stripe on the face.  The underparts were a medium-gray color and apparently unmarked.  I saw only the leading edge and some of the side of the wings, yet I was able to note that the coverts and remiges were dark gray with lighter gray fringes that extended down the edges and across the tips of the greater coverts to create a pattern or elongate rectangles.  The remiges were similarly marked, but because I was unable to see the tips of these feathers I thought the pattern was one of well-defined stripes along the leading edge of the wing.  The bil appeared to be entirely dull black and the legs were pale.  I saw this bird’s eyes, but I cannot now recall their coloration.--The young birds were quite a dark shade of gray above and dull whitish below with bold streaks of about the same shade of dark gray as the upperparts.  I noted on at least one of these birds a pattern on the wing coverts and remiges that was much like that of the adult, but with the centers of the feathers even darker and the fringes maybe not so purely light gray.  The head was generally quite dark but also with a somewhat streaked appearance.  As I recall, both of these birds had entirely black bills, but I cannot recall noting the color of the eyes or legs in the field.

I arrived in the Del Rey Lagoon parking lot on the evening of 6 June 2015 at around 3:45 p.m. (2245 Zulu) and found Jim Lomax and Curtis Marantz standing in the shade of a ficus tree, dressed in entirely inappropriate clothing for Southern California beach weather (standard-issue birding green fleece sweaters, khaki pants with cargo pockets, et cetera) . They were debating what method they would use to find the bird: stay and wait, or walk around, hoping to find the bird elsewhere. Realizing that I would need to carpe avem, I walked back to my 2003 Toyota Celica GT (4 cylinder, 36 mpg) for the purpose of doffing my Birkenstocks, and donning my Nike running shoes, as I would soon find myself climbing on irregularly shaped (rhomboids, polyhedrons, ovoid trapezoids, etc.) rocks along Ballona Creek. The Dodgers t-shirt and black running shorts were staying.--Alas, this would prove unnecessary, after I casually raised my glass one last time, and pointed it at the concrete dike at the north end of the lagoon. At the very same spot that I had repeatedly scanned yesterday, Friday, and today, Saturday, the Yellow-crowned Night Heron had magically appeared, without any of us seeing it fly in. column51: List maintained by Mark Holmgren. Coverage: I can’t specify the areas that we (in 5 cars) were led to by Martin Ruane, Base Biologist. However, we visually ‘reached into’ the Ventura County Game Preserve by driving along its extensive fenced boundary with the naval station. We made about 9 stops scoping the ocean, the primary inlet channel, the night-heron roost, several parts of the tidal marsh, dry runway margins, open dry fields, and briefly the neighborhood south of the entrance. Conspicuously Absent or Scarce: no Canada or other geese; Gadwall and teal (we probably did not focus well enough into the game preserve); more Mourning Dove; Cassin's Kingbird; American Crow; more Western Scrub-Jays; Bewick's Wren; Wrentit; Hermit Thrush; other sparrows, though we did not get a chance to study flocks; we saw very few Red-winged Blackbird; Great-tailed Grackle; Brown-headed Cowbird.

Entered via a trail from the Brightwater development near the corner of Kennybunk Lane and Oceanridge Drive. This trail (if you take it straight from the entry path, not turning right or left as you enter it) takes you directly down to the area where the bird has been seen (channel and muted tidal basin). The bird was under the bridge which crosses the channel. Bird was shy, and I only got two pictures off before it flew across the channel landing on a submerged log near the distant northerly shore of the muted tidal basin.----I was surprised by the amount of yellow in this juvenile bird's lower bill (see pic, below) which seemed in size/shape more akin to a Black-crowned Night-Heron. But the similarity with the Black-crowned stopped there. ----The bird (after landing across the tidal basin) spent a while peering around exhibiting its long neck; distinctly different from Black-crowned. The wing coverts had small spots, as did the back of the bird versus the larger spots of Black-crowned. Red eye, yellowish (sort of yellowish green to my eye) legs and longer legs than Black-crowned. Brown breast streaking was more clean and distinct than a Black-crowned.----

column52: As I walked up the channel path I noticed a night heron sitting obscured in the shadow of the footbridge over the Wintersburg Channel. I initially could only see a backlit silhouette but from some distance away I could make out a heavy, blunt tipped bill. As I got closer I could see fine white triangular tips to the slate colored wing feathers, not the broad white tips typical of Black-crowneds. ----I moved to sunward of the bridge to get in better light and study the bird in greater detail. The bill was a dark grey color except for a thin yellow band running along the bottom of the bill from tip to base. The eye was red. The lores were a dull white. The head and breast were the same slate color as the wings and extensively covered in thin white streaks. The legs were yellow and notably long in proportion to the body.----This marks the 3rd consecutive year a juvenile Yellow-crowned has appeared in the Wintersburg Channel near the bridge. All these birds have appeared from mid July to early August.

column52: **First SLO County Record** one photographed yesterday by Linda Dalton and posted to slocobirding listserv this morning. Both birds appeared to be young of the year. One was at the east end of the marina and the other was first seen around mid-marina and then flew and roosted in a cypress tree below the State Park Museum, just above and to the west of the restrooms across the the kayak rentals. Both birds seen and photographed by many observers. Compared to Black-crowned Night-Heron, these birds seemed slimmer and larger billed. The stout bills were almost all dark except for some yellow , mostly at the base of the lower mandibles. Wing coverts showed white spots at tips (photos show them to be more like triangles) and thin white edges. Chin pale, unstreaked and with a yellow tinge and head somewhat dark and finely streaked. column52: Guy located the resident night-herons within minutes of our arrival at the park today.  We then spent several minutes studying these birds and taking a few photos before continuing on our way.  All of the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that we saw today were in a single, broadleaf tree located over the parking lot in the northwestern part of the park.  We saw at least two adults standing atop nests and one or two additional nests located not far from where other birds were perched in the tree.  In all, we saw six adult birds and one first-winter individual.  I took photos of at least one of these birds, but I studied the others at least relatively carefully.  Below is a composite description of what I noted on the various adults during this encounter.--These were medium-sized herons with stocky bodies, large heads, and massive bills that tapered from a base that was both wide and deep to a blunt tip.  Given that we were looking up at these birds, it was difficult to discern their precise shape, but my impression was that the crown was relatively flattened and I noted on at least one or two of these birds one or two filamentous plumes extending back from the nape.  These birds also appeared to have relatively short wings that extended roughly to the tip of the tail, and medium-length legs that were at least moderately stout.--The adults were generally a medium-gray color overall and with little or no markings on the underparts.  Rather striking was a head pattern that combined a butter-yellow forehead with a creamy to whitish crown and a complementary band of white across the lower part of the face.  Contrasting with the pale regions of the face was the black of the lower and rear parts of the head and the superciliary region.  I noted on at least one bird one or two filamentous, white plumes extended back from the nape.  The wing coverts and remiges were dark gray with well-defined edges of light gray to whitish that produced a boldly striped pattern to the wings overall.  Given that I was looking up at these birds, I am not sure how well I ever saw their backs, but even if I did, I cannot now recall much about them.  I noted that the bill of each bird on which I saw it clearly was mostly black, but I am not sure the degree to which the base of the lower mandible may have been paler.  I also have only a vague recollection that the eyes were dark and that the legs were greenish.--The immature bird was a medium to dark gray in color, but quite dingy overall, and with a somewhat mottled appearance below.  This bird also had whitish to pale gray fringes to the wing coverts and remiges that resulted in a somewhat striped pattern, yet one that was more subtle than that on the adults as a result of the edges appearing worn and relatively thin.  This bird also had at least one white plume extending back from the nape, and its overall size and structure were similar to those of the adults.  I noted on this bird that the eyes were an odd shade of orange.  The bill was at least mostly black, but again, I am not sure to what degree the lower mandible may have been paler.

column52: Guy located the resident night-herons within minutes of our arrival at the park today.  We then spent several minutes studying these birds and taking a few photos before continuing on our way.  All of the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that we saw today were in a single, broadleaf tree located over the parking lot in the northwestern part of the park.  We saw at least two adults standing atop nests and one or two additional nests located not far from where other birds were perched in the tree.  In all, we saw six adult birds and one first-winter individual.  I took photos of at least one of these birds, but I studied the others at least relatively carefully.  Below is a composite description of what I noted on the various adults during this encounter.--These were medium-sized herons with stocky bodies, large heads, and massive bills that tapered from a base that was both wide and deep to a blunt tip.  Given that we were looking up at these birds, it was difficult to discern their precise shape, but my impression was that the crown was relatively flattened and I noted on at least one or two of these birds one or two filamentous plumes extending back from the nape.  These birds also appeared to have relatively short wings that extended roughly to the tip of the tail, and medium-length legs that were at least moderately stout.--The adults were generally a medium-gray color overall and with little or no markings on the underparts.  Rather striking was a head pattern that combined a butter-yellow forehead with a creamy to whitish crown and a complementary band of white across the lower part of the face.  Contrasting with the pale regions of the face was the black of the lower and rear parts of the head and the superciliary region.  I noted on at least one bird one or two filamentous, white plumes extended back from the nape.  The wing coverts and remiges were dark gray with well-defined edges of light gray to whitish that produced a boldly striped pattern to the wings overall.  Given that I was looking up at these birds, I am not sure how well I ever saw their backs, but even if I did, I cannot now recall much about them.  I noted that the bill of each bird on which I saw it clearly was mostly black, but I am not sure the degree to which the base of the lower mandible may have been paler.  I also have only a vague recollection that the eyes were dark and that the legs were greenish.--The immature bird was a medium to dark gray in color, but quite dingy overall, and with a somewhat mottled appearance below.  This bird also had whitish to pale gray fringes to the wing coverts and remiges that resulted in a somewhat striped pattern, yet one that was more subtle than that on the adults as a result of the edges appearing worn and relatively thin.  This bird also had at least one white plume extending back from the nape, and its overall size and structure were similar to those of the adults.  I noted on this bird that the eyes were an odd shade of orange.  The bill was at least mostly black, but again, I am not sure to what degree the lower mandible may have been paler.

column51: Curtis Marantz and I quickly walked the marina near dusk looking for the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons reported here. We saw one, the bird with typical patterning for juvenile Yellow-crown. Light fog; strong breeze 10-15 mph W; tide mid to low and rising; quick check of the marina.
column52: Perched on a boat at the western end of the marina where several Black-crowned Night-Herons also were perched. Even in the dim light, this bird was a cold gray color overall with crisp streaking in the face and on the underparts. The crown was likewise streaked with thin pale lines but on a blacker background. The streaks on the underparts were sharply blackish against a whitish background. I noted that the greater wing coverts were tipped with small dots of white and the outer margin of these coverts was thinly but distinctly margined with pale cream or white, this forming a lattice-like pattern across the wing. The remaining wing coverts and scapulars were also tipped with small white dots. I did note that the pattern in the very midline back was more obscure and that the actual back feathers were plainer gray, with perhaps only the tiniest of white dots. This is typical of Yellow-crowned Night-Heron. (This bird, however, was not the one of two here that has freshly molted back feathers that are plain.)----The bird appeared smaller and particularly of slighter, rangier build than a juvenile Black-crowned nearby. The bill was blunt and thick and all black (or nearly all black so that in this light I could not see any obvious pale coloration at the base of the mandible). The rear end of the bird appeared to sit higher on the legs versus Black-crowned, which when squat has its rear (tip of tail) further down the legs. This made the Yellow-crowned look taller, even though I could not assess the actual leg length difference. The bill of Black-crowned was clearly longer, tapered to a sharp tip, and slightly decurved. The Black-crowned also showed obvious pale on most of the mandible.----Nothing about the features of this bird suggested past hybridization with Black-crowned. One Yellow-crowned Night-Heron was first reported here 13 September by Linda Dalton (fide Tom Edell). Two were then seen on the 14th. These constitute the first record of this species for San Luis Obispo County and one of only three records north of Santa Barbara County in California (San Rafael, Marin Co. from mid July 1968 continuing/returning through mid Oct 1973; 12 Sep-17 Oct 1981 at Año Nuevo State Reserve, San Mateo Co.; two reports not accepted from northern CA include birds at Tomales Bay, Marin Co., and at Bodega Bay, Sonoma Co.; there is also a report not accepted from Furnace Creek, Inyo Co., per Hamilton et al. 2007).

column51: Trip Leader: Nancy Kenyon Tide: 4.1 ft. High tide at 9:32 AM; 2.0 ft Low tide at 2:45 PM--Skipper: Robert Sloan Counters: Jeff Bray, Sally Menzel, Sharon Harrow, Darrell Wilson, Mark Kincheloe,--Chuck Nichols, Sandy Smith, Jan Wilson, and Nancy Kenyon.--Comments: We had perfect weather for our trip; it was comfortably warm and the sky was overcast with no breeze.--There was no glare and the colors of the birds’ plumage stood out well against the mud flats and vegetation along the--shore. For most of the trip, the water was so calm that we were able to enjoy perfect reflections of the shoreline.--We saw several species of raptors: 7 Ospreys, two of which were calling back and forth to each other from across the--channel; a kestrel was perched on the Osprey’s nesting platform by the Back-Bay Science Center; 2 White-tailed Kites--were near each other in a tree; a Northern Harrier was chasing a flock of Willets in flight; and a Red-tailed Hawk was--perched high on the side of a cliff overlooking the bay.--The Least and Western Sandpipers must have arrived recently; they were still in enormous flocks tightly massed--together on the mudflats. When a flock took off in flight, it was like a glimmering cloud. Since the tide was still high,--there weren’t any spacious mud flats from which they could feed. There were lots of Black-bellied Plovers massed on--top of the Santa Ynez Spit as well as on a couple of mud flats and many still had black bellies. Other shorebirds--included Whimbrels, Long-billed Curlews, Marbled Godwits, Short-billed Dowitchers, Spotted Sandpipers, and Willets.--Barn Swallows were swooping overhead catching insects. Western Gulls were all over the place. Large Mullets were--leaping out of the water. Caspian Terns were resting in their usual spot right below the Science Center, their red bills--prominent in the soft lighting. In the little bay past the Caspian Terns, we were thrilled to spot a juvenile Yellow-crowned--Night Heron feeding on crabs at the water’s edge. We sat in the boat watching him for quite a while and he paid no--attention to us. There were a number of Snowy Egrets singly and in groups all the way along. The Black Skimmers were--still inhabiting the upper part of the bay in giant flocks, many on the ground, some flying around and we could hear their--distinctive cry from quite a distance. On the way back, we watched with amusement as a Great Blue Heron stood on--the shore quite close to a fisherman, waiting for a chance to grab his fish when he pulled it out of the water.--Unfortunately we were unable to linger to find out who got the fish.

column51: Trip Leader: Nancy Kenyon Tide: 4.1 ft. High tide at 9:32 AM; 2.0 ft Low tide at 2:45 PM--Skipper: Robert Sloan Counters: Jeff Bray, Sally Menzel, Sharon Harrow, Darrell Wilson, Mark Kincheloe,--Chuck Nichols, Sandy Smith, Jan Wilson, and Nancy Kenyon.--Comments: We had perfect weather for our trip; it was comfortably warm and the sky was overcast with no breeze.--There was no glare and the colors of the birds’ plumage stood out well against the mud flats and vegetation along the--shore. For most of the trip, the water was so calm that we were able to enjoy perfect reflections of the shoreline.--We saw several species of raptors: 7 Ospreys, two of which were calling back and forth to each other from across the--channel; a kestrel was perched on the Osprey’s nesting platform by the Back-Bay Science Center; 2 White-tailed Kites--were near each other in a tree; a Northern Harrier was chasing a flock of Willets in flight; and a Red-tailed Hawk was--perched high on the side of a cliff overlooking the bay.--The Least and Western Sandpipers must have arrived recently; they were still in enormous flocks tightly massed--together on the mudflats. When a flock took off in flight, it was like a glimmering cloud. Since the tide was still high,--there weren’t any spacious mud flats from which they could feed. There were lots of Black-bellied Plovers massed on--top of the Santa Ynez Spit as well as on a couple of mud flats and many still had black bellies. Other shorebirds--included Whimbrels, Long-billed Curlews, Marbled Godwits, Short-billed Dowitchers, Spotted Sandpipers, and Willets.--Barn Swallows were swooping overhead catching insects. Western Gulls were all over the place. Large Mullets were--leaping out of the water. Caspian Terns were resting in their usual spot right below the Science Center, their red bills--prominent in the soft lighting. In the little bay past the Caspian Terns, we were thrilled to spot a juvenile Yellow-crowned--Night Heron feeding on crabs at the water’s edge. We sat in the boat watching him for quite a while and he paid no--attention to us. There were a number of Snowy Egrets singly and in groups all the way along. The Black Skimmers were--still inhabiting the upper part of the bay in giant flocks, many on the ground, some flying around and we could hear their--distinctive cry from quite a distance. On the way back, we watched with amusement as a Great Blue Heron stood on--the shore quite close to a fisherman, waiting for a chance to grab his fish when he pulled it out of the water.--Unfortunately we were unable to linger to find out who got the fish.

column52: Continuing under the Franklin Creek footbridge.

This was a boldly marked bird with the head pattern dominating the patterns.  The forehead and forecrown were rich, butter-yellow in color blending to a creamy-yellow to whitish as it tapered and extended back across the crown to the nape.  The longest plumes were white, but I thought some of the shorter plumes may have been dark.  Contrasting sharply with the paler forehead and crown, the lores, supraloral and superciliary regions, and the lower parts of the face were a dull black in color.  Complementing the cream-colored crown was a comma-shaped band of this same color that began narrowly right under the eye and then extended more broadly backward across the auriculars before ending in a rounded terminus at the rear edge of the auriculars.  Below the whitish stripe, the lower part of the face and the throat were again dull black, as was the side of the upper neck immediately behind the auriculars.  Demarcating the boldly marked head, the neck was an unmarked, medium-gray color down to the breast and back.  The underparts were this same medium-gray from the breast and sides down across the belly, flanks, and probably the undertail coverts, though my recollection of the latter is not as good.  I also noted a few dusky streaks on the belly that were relatively inconspicuous, yet bolder than I can recall seeing on this species in the past.--Returning to the upperparts, the coloration of the back and wings combined slate-gray to blackish centers with medium-gray fringes.  On the back and scapulars, the feathers were slate-gray to dull blackish with medium-gray edges that were well-defined and of roughly comparable width from the base to the tip of each tapered feather, which resulted in a series of V-shaped markings.  Further apparent were several long, conspicuously narrow, and filamentous plumes that extended almost to the wingtips and which again had slate-gray to blackish shaft-stripes that contrasted with medium-gray edges that had a frayed appearance.  The rather small lesser-coverts near the shoulder had slate-gray centers that contrasted with narrow but well-defined fringes that created a scaly pattern.  The coloration of the medina coverts was similar, but their larger size and more tapered shape resulted in two or three rows of V-shaped markings across the middle part of the wing.  The greater coverts, however, had slate-gray centers that contrasted with a light gray fringe along the outer web of each feather but a much weaker edge to the inner web to create a row of sharply defined stripes along the lower, middle part of the wing.  I am not sure I ever clearly saw the primary coverts, but there were some dull, blackish feathers along the leading edge of the wing that presumably represented the alula and associated feathers.  Also apparent was what appeared to be more whitish, marginal wing-coverts that appeared as a band of whitish extending along leaving edge of the slightly spread wing.  I thought the pattern on the tertials and maybe one or two of the innermost secondaries was like that on the greater coverts, given narrow fringes of light gray contrasting sharply with slate-gray to blackish centers, but my impression was that the fringes on these feathers extended the length of both the inner and outer webs and around the tip of each feather.  The remaining remiges, representing most of the secondaries and seemingly all of the primaries, were again dusky gray to sooty in color, but these feathers had only inconspicuously paler edges to the outer webs that appeared more brownish of buffy in color.  I noted both that the tail was dark and that it did not contrast strongly with the closed wings, but I saw no more detail than this.--The bill was entirely black from base to tip, the eyes were a deep reddish-orange in color and surrounded by a dark orbital-ring, and the legs were a dull yellowish color when seen from behind and on the toes, but from the front, the legs were a dusky grayish in color.

column51: SWBSC field trip led by base naturalist, Martin Ruane.  27 participants.

Trip Leader: Nancy Kenyon Tide: 4.1 ft. High tide at 9:32 AM; 2.0 ft Low tide at 2:45 PM--Skipper: Robert Sloan Counters: Jeff Bray, Sally Menzel, Sharon Harrow, Darrell Wilson, Mark Kincheloe,--Chuck Nichols, Sandy Smith, Jan Wilson, and Nancy Kenyon.--Comments: We had perfect weather for our trip; it was comfortably warm and the sky was overcast with no breeze.--There was no glare and the colors of the birds’ plumage stood out well against the mud flats and vegetation along the--shore. For most of the trip, the water was so calm that we were able to enjoy perfect reflections of the shoreline.--We saw several species of raptors: 7 Ospreys, two of which were calling back and forth to each other from across the--channel; a kestrel was perched on the Osprey’s nesting platform by the Back-Bay Science Center; 2 White-tailed Kites--were near each other in a tree; a Northern Harrier was chasing a flock of Willets in flight; and a Red-tailed Hawk was--perched high on the side of a cliff overlooking the bay.--The Least and Western Sandpipers must have arrived recently; they were still in enormous flocks tightly massed--together on the mudflats. When a flock took off in flight, it was like a glimmering cloud. Since the tide was still high,--there weren’t any spacious mud flats from which they could feed. There were lots of Black-bellied Plovers massed on--top of the Santa Ynez Spit as well as on a couple of mud flats and many still had black bellies. Other shorebirds--included Whimbrels, Long-billed Curlews, Marbled Godwits, Short-billed Dowitchers, Spotted Sandpipers, and Willets.--Barn Swallows were swooping overhead catching insects. Western Gulls were all over the place. Large Mullets were--leaping out of the water. Caspian Terns were resting in their usual spot right below the Science Center, their red bills--prominent in the soft lighting. In the little bay past the Caspian Terns, we were thrilled to spot a juvenile Yellow-crowned--Night Heron feeding on crabs at the water’s edge. We sat in the boat watching him for quite a while and he paid no--attention to us. There were a number of Snowy Egrets singly and in groups all the way along. The Black Skimmers were--still inhabiting the upper part of the bay in giant flocks, many on the ground, some flying around and we could hear their--distinctive cry from quite a distance. On the way back, we watched with amusement as a Great Blue Heron stood on--the shore quite close to a fisherman, waiting for a chance to grab his fish when he pulled it out of the water.--Unfortunately we were unable to linger to find out who got the fish.

column52: Given that Dick had already located the continuing night-heron prior to our arrival, we had no problem seeing this bird as soon as we arrived in the vicinity of the boat docks.  We spent a few minutes looking at this bird and I took a few photos as it perched in to open on a dead branch immediately across the lake, but it moved out of sight after only a few minutes.  I relocated the heron a few minutes later as it perched in a more obscured location on or near the same branch but in the shade amid the vegetation of the willows, where it remained for the duration of our visit.  The views through my scope were good, but the distance was a bit much for good photos, especially when the bird was partially obscured.--This was a medium-sized heron with a blocky head, stocky body, seemingly short wings, relatively long and moderately stout legs, and a generally heavy bill that was a little longer than the head was wide and tapering from a deep base to a pointed tip along a subtly yet smoothly decurved culmen.  I further noted that the forehead was short and inconspicuous, and that the crown was gently rounded to somewhat flattened with a short plume extending back from the rear terminus of the crown, but given that this bird was in a relaxed position with the neck retracted, it was impossible to gain an appreciation of the length or mass or the neck, and some of the details of the head shape.  I also failed to notice in detail the primary projection and placement of the wingtips relative to the tail when this bird was facing away from me, yet my impression was that the wings were short and rounded, with minimal primary projection and wingtips that were about as long as the tail--This was a relatively boldly marked bird that was generally typical of an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron in its patterns and coloration.  I noted, for example, that the head was almost entirely a dull black in color, including the supraloral and superciliary regions, the lower part of the face, and the entire throat.  Contrasting sharply with the mostly black head was a subtly curved, creamy-white crescent that extended back from a point just below the eye across the auriculars, curving upward and expanding slightly as it crossed the lower part of the auriculars to their rear terminus.  Somewhat atypical for an adult of this species, the forehead and crown were mostly blackish centrally, yet with narrow lines of cream to pale yellowish extending along either side of the forehead and crown and tapering inward to frame the dark center of the crown.  I also thought the plume that extended backward from the rear part of the crown was dark as opposed to white.  The black-and-whitish head was sharply demarcated by a medium-gray neck that appeared to lack markings altogether.  The underparts were similarly colored, but I noted a few relatively fine, dark streaks on the belly that I do not usually associate with an adult of this species.--Returning to the upperparts, what I could see of the back, scapulars, and wing coverts appeared to have a strong pattern that combined blackish centers to feathers that had narrow yet well-defined edges of light gray that tapered inward distally as a result of what appeared to be generally wedge-shaped feathers.  I did not see the remiges quite as well as the coverts, but what I did see appeared to combine dark gray centers with edges that were weaker than those of the coverts either because they were narrower or not as pale a gray.--The bill was mostly black, but with a paler and possibly yellowish stripe that extended maybe halfway out the center of the lower mandible.  The irides were either reddish or orangey-red and thus contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs and toes appeared to be a relatively dark gray to grayish-horn in color, though there may have been some yellowish tones to the “knee” joints.

Geez, it would have been nice to know that this place is fenced off, and locked, with no Public Access (but there are at least 2 Italian restaurants across the street, a possible consolation). This is an adult Night Heron with a very dark grey body. The head is large and fat, compared to the head of a black-crowned night heron. The head has thick black and white horizontal stripes in the face, and a yellow crown. The bird has a thick crab-eating bill, clearly different in shape from that of a black-crowned night heron. column52: With the recent adult in Sac I checked EBird and noticed one I found years ago was not in ebird:  Juvenile Yellow-crowned Night-Heron — Sacramento, Summer 2019. Rare bird for the region. Initially undocumented on checklist while awaiting photo review and confirmation. Now submitted with multiple clear images.--Field Marks Supporting YCNH over juvenile Black-crowned Night-Heron:- • Head and Bill: Thick, blunt bill with a slightly paler base and prominent reddish-orange eye, diagnostic for Yellow-crowned. Black-crowned juveniles typically show a slimmer, more tapered bill and duller eyes.- • Plumage: Coarse, bold vertical streaking on the neck and underparts, as well as finely barred coverts on the upper wings. The streaks on this bird are buffy and broad — not the narrower, more teardrop-shaped streaking seen on BCNH.- • Posture and Proportions: Bird held a more elongated neck, taller stance, and upright posture typical of Yellow-crowned. BCNH usually appears stockier and more hunched, with a shorter neck.- • Flight Structure: In-flight shots show broad, rounded wings with minimal contrast between inner and outer flight feathers, and longer, dangling legs. Yellow-crowned typically shows a more uniform wing coloration than BCNH

column52: Two young birds, one looked clearly to be an HY, and the other seemed likely to have been a 2Y.. The HY clearly had the juvenile wing pattern, with the white-tipped greater coverts with thin white exposed edges. The crown was a bit darker than than the rest of the head, but it didn't show the adult head pattern. The upperparts were a flat gray, but the scapulars had darker feather centers, but not contrastingly so. The bird was paler below with blurry gray streaking. The other, presumably older, bird did not show the juvenile wing pattern or the blurry steaks on the underside (that I could tell). It was darker on the crown than the younger bird, but also didn't appear to have a real hint of the adult head pattern. It was the same color gray above as the younger bird, also with uncontrastingly darker centers to the scapulars, but with similarly darker greater coverts. Both had the longer legs than Black-crowned, with much of the tibia visible.----Note added 11/11/2019. Looking at Don Thornton's photos, I believe these are probably the same age after all, although the described plumage differences are mostly right. However, both birds show hints of the adult head pattern. If I understand the molt and plumages of this species, these are both HY birds in 1st basic.----Note added 12/1/2019: a review of birds photographed at this location clearly shows that these birds were molting from juv to 1st basic plumage in September. These are clearly HY birds.

column52: Compared to other night-herons present in the willow patch on the north side of the lagoon, this bird was over all grayish in tone, although breast was not well seen.  I viewed it by spotting scope from the south side of the lagoon looking north. The bird was at 34.40877 -119.84605. Bill was slightly stubbier than other herons present and grayish-black with minimal pale color at the base of the mandible. Those breast streaks that are visible seem thin and not blurry.  Spots on the wings seem small and round, not tear-drop shaped. The greater wing coverts show a white margin on their outer edge. Perhaps this is the first sighting for Campus Lagoon.  The other night-herons present should be checked more carefully than I was able to do today.

column52: While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

column51: Tom Edell, Curtis Marantz, Wes Fritz, and Will Knowlton led the full-day pelagic trip for the Morro Bay Winter Bird Festival aboard the M/V Endeavor out of the Morro Bay Landing with Brad Leage as captain.  The present list is for our return trip through the harbor and inshore waters out to the outermost buoy at the mouth of the harbor.  We cruised through the harbor relatively quickly, so even though we did our best to see what was present, this is best considered an incomplete survey of the many birds that were present on a relatively low tide with exposed mudflats along the sandspit.  We arrived at the dock at 3:25 pm, but then spent an extended period of time at the dock going over the lists for the day.  We saw both Long-tailed Ducks, but we did not stop to study either of them carefully.  The obvious highlight, but seen by only the leaders at the dock after participants had left, was an immature Yellow-crowned Night-Heron that was spotted by Fritz at the dock.  Also onboard were local birders Maggie Smith, Herb Elliott, and Pat and Ann Vaughan, Jeff Miller, Norman Pillsbury, but most participants were from out of town.  Edell's eBird Android phone app calculated the one-way distance through the harbor at 1.42 miles.  There was a roughly 95% cover of high clouds, a moderate (10-15 knot), breeze from the northeast, from which we were largely sheltered when at the dock, and a temperature of 57° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Edell’s vehicle).  3:10-4:00 pm.----Sea Otter - 18 (this is an estimate).
column52: While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

column51: Conejo Valley Audubon field trip. When we did arrive at the lagoon, the tide was still relatively high and our shorebird numbers and species diversity were low as a result. A brief seawatch produced the continuing Red-necked Grebe off the lagoon mouth. Weather was sunny, 49F (at 0800), winds ENE 3 mph.
