column52: Adult at water's edge between the bridges: Wide creamy crown strip and cheek patch surrounded by black; thick dark bill; slate gray body. Subadult just east of bridge construction: no prominent head pattern; thick bill; more gray than brown body (not speckled juvenile).

While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

column51: Tom Edell, Curtis Marantz, Wes Fritz, and Will Knowlton led the full-day pelagic trip for the Morro Bay Winter Bird Festival aboard the M/V Endeavor out of the Morro Bay Landing with Brad Leage as captain.  The present list is for our return trip through the harbor and inshore waters out to the outermost buoy at the mouth of the harbor.  We cruised through the harbor relatively quickly, so even though we did our best to see what was present, this is best considered an incomplete survey of the many birds that were present on a relatively low tide with exposed mudflats along the sandspit.  We arrived at the dock at 3:25 pm, but then spent an extended period of time at the dock going over the lists for the day.  We saw both Long-tailed Ducks, but we did not stop to study either of them carefully.  The obvious highlight, but seen by only the leaders at the dock after participants had left, was an immature Yellow-crowned Night-Heron that was spotted by Fritz at the dock.  Also onboard were local birders Maggie Smith, Herb Elliott, and Pat and Ann Vaughan, Jeff Miller, Norman Pillsbury, but most participants were from out of town.  Edell's eBird Android phone app calculated the one-way distance through the harbor at 1.42 miles.  There was a roughly 95% cover of high clouds, a moderate (10-15 knot), breeze from the northeast, from which we were largely sheltered when at the dock, and a temperature of 57° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Edell’s vehicle).  3:10-4:00 pm.----Sea Otter - 18 (this is an estimate).
column52: While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

column51: Tom Edell, Curtis Marantz, Wes Fritz, and Will Knowlton led the full-day pelagic trip for the Morro Bay Winter Bird Festival aboard the M/V Endeavor out of the Morro Bay Landing with Brad Leage as captain.  The present list is for our return trip through the harbor and inshore waters out to the outermost buoy at the mouth of the harbor.  We cruised through the harbor relatively quickly, so even though we did our best to see what was present, this is best considered an incomplete survey of the many birds that were present on a relatively low tide with exposed mudflats along the sandspit.  We arrived at the dock at 3:25 pm, but then spent an extended period of time at the dock going over the lists for the day.  We saw both Long-tailed Ducks, but we did not stop to study either of them carefully.  The obvious highlight, but seen by only the leaders at the dock after participants had left, was an immature Yellow-crowned Night-Heron that was spotted by Fritz at the dock.  Also onboard were local birders Maggie Smith, Herb Elliott, and Pat and Ann Vaughan, Jeff Miller, Norman Pillsbury, but most participants were from out of town.  Edell's eBird Android phone app calculated the one-way distance through the harbor at 1.42 miles.  There was a roughly 95% cover of high clouds, a moderate (10-15 knot), breeze from the northeast, from which we were largely sheltered when at the dock, and a temperature of 57° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Edell’s vehicle).  3:10-4:00 pm.----Sea Otter - 18 (this is an estimate).
column52: While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird. Weather was partly cloudy most of the day, with wind from the west (up to 10 mph) and temperatures in the 50s (degrees F). The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils. column52: While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts. column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual winter pelagic trip on January 11, 2020 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Mike Bursk as captain. We departed the dock and cruised along both sides of the west jetty in Dana Point Harbor scanning for gulls and shorebirds, then travelled northwest along the coast over the 100-fathom curve. Upon reaching Newport Canyons we headed west toward the offshore oil platforms (Eureka, Ellen, and Edith), then south toward Lausen Sea Mount. After arriving at the high point of the sea mount, we finally turned east back toward Dana Point Harbor. Weather was partly cloudy most of the day, with wind from the west (up to 10 mph) and temperatures in the 50s (degrees F). This list covers birds seen just outside Dana Point Harbor and inside the harbor back to the dock.

While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual winter pelagic trip on January 11, 2020 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Mike Bursk as captain. Trip leaders were Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Jeff Bray, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. We departed the dock and cruised along both sides of the west jetty in Dana Point Harbor scanning for gulls and shorebirds, then travelled northwest along the coast over the 100-fathom curve. Upon reaching Newport Canyons we headed west toward the offshore oil platforms (Eureka, Ellen, and Edith), then south toward Lausen Sea Mount. After arriving at the high point of the sea mount, we finally turned east back toward Dana Point Harbor. Weather was partly cloudy most of the day, with wind from the west (up to 10 mph) and temperatures in the 50s (degrees F). This list covers birds seen just outside Dana Point Harbor and inside the harbor back to the dock.

column51: A late afternoon trip as we saw it was a low tide and I wanted to try out the new camera lens I had just rented. The afternoon was cloudy and intermittently sprinkling. At one point the wind picked up and rain started coming down harder so we almost left but decided to keep going. We were rewarded with clearing clouds and many excellent sightings with a glorious sunset later on. Walking just past the Least Tern colony a Western Meadowlark was foraging on the bank alongside the inner bay, with many Brant calling from the water adjacent to the colony. On the cement bridge crossing over the channel, many Ring-billed Gulls were dropping mussels to crack them open and eat them. A small group of female ducks including 2 Lesser Scaup, 1 Ruddy Duck, and 1 Bufflehead were swimming between the bridge and the floating barrier in the channel. A female Common Goldeneye was swimming in the same area with her head and neck in the water and only her eyes above water. Further on down the channel we had the nice surprise of a Eurasian Wigeon amongst all the American Wigeons. On our way out while walking across the boardwalk during sunset, we spotted a Ridgway's Rail that James had heard call earlier. We were treated to great looks of this bird pulling fish out of the mud in one location, then running to another location to eat the fish. After doing this a few times the bird then took a bath to rinse off all the mud that had accumulated!

Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Campo Pachico fishing village (26.80252 x 113.147) is where there are a mangrove island with a heronry and an Osprey nest atop a nearby roof. Then we headed toward potential campsites (Kuyima and Antonio’s), both of which were closed. But we birded the fairly short mangroves nearby on foot, finding Mangrove Yellow Warblers and Ridgeway’s Rails. Then we explored to the tip of the peninsula, where we found slightly higher-statue mangroves and lots of shorebirds feeding in the bay at low tide. We decided to camp here. It was good for the rails, the warblers, and Belding’s Savanna Sparrows. And we saw an impressive migration of swallows (including Purple Martins) and 2 Green Herons just before sunset.

Started at small parking lot at PCH took inner bay loop trail and then down the Wintersburg Channel to the Bolsa Pocket and back to Rabbit Island Overlook at which point I completed the count so as not to repeat birds I had already seen.  Hi Tide was 1034.  I did not see the Juvenile Bald Eagle that I had seen two days prior back by the pocket but I got a really good look at the Little Blue Heron, two Common Golden Eyes back by the Pocket and also the Yellow Crowned Night Heron.  I could see the adult clearly in my binoculars from the innerbay loop (and have a really poor quality pic due to distance and the gray day but it clearly shows the Bold Black and White head pattern with a yellow crown stripe and very thick bill.  When I walked around the PCH side the adult was obscured by the foliage but I did get a close up of what appeared to be an immature yellow  and not black crowned night heron.  I was leaning toward immature Black crowned night heron when I saw it from across the pond based on his shape but his bill looked really beefy and just didn't look as pointy as the juvenile black crowned night herons I have seen plus the likelihood of it being another Yellow crowned seemed really low.  I couldn't see any large white spots on his wing coverts (or narrow distinct streaks vs blurry streaks of black crowned) from a distance and the feathers appeared to be a dark taupe color but my vantage point was poor.  It didn't look particularly slender like I expected a yellow crowned to look but I didn't see it in flight or with wings (or neck) extended away from body either.  I would have put it in a basic  yellow crowned/black crowned category if I could because of my uncertainty but there wasn't one.  Please let me know how I should record this.
column52: I observed the adult yellow crowned night heron in my binoculars  from across on the inner bay loop trail in the brush with a black crowned night heron about 10 feet away to the left and another heron about equidistant on the right.  All three were hunkered down with their necks not extended.   The Yellow crowned in the center had a very bold black and white head pattern with obvious white cheek patches, and a thick yellow band across his crown with  thick darker bill.  I have several  horrible pics too distant for my lens and a very gray day but I will put it in to help ID since its uncommon.  I walked around the PCH side to get a closer look and was able to get a good look at the Black Crowned but the Yellow Crowned adult was deeper in the foliage with only a portion of his  back in view.  I was however able to get a  good look  at the bird at the far right of what appears to be an immature yellow crowned night heron - with a very thick dark gray black bill, yellow under it on its throat.  He had yellowish gray legs but I couldn't see his feet from this vantage point and from across the pond in binoculars it was hard to tell his leg length and overall appearance of its neck length, look to see if it was more slender, lankier than the black crowned and I couldn't see the streaking under its throat from the inner loop trail  to see if it was narrow and distinct or broad and blurry like a black crowned.  I have a pic I will submit so someone can confirm yellow crowned vs black crowned immature.  He was hunkered down so I really didn't see him move, forage or extend his wings.  Darker gray feathers on his back and no spots were visible.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Stop 7 of Big Day. Right when we arrived a young Peregrine Falcon was flying over the bay, flushing terns and shorebirds from the small islands. It forced a flying Caspian Tern into the water but didn't catch anything. Later on in the channel we saw it again, diving multiple times at ducks. A Merlin flying over rabbit island dove towards and flushed a Northern Harrier. We had great luck here, turning up multiple duck species we haven't seen here yet this fall, seeing an adult Yellow-crowned Night Heron, having more Lesser Yellowlegs than we have ever had here before, scrounged up a Dunlin mixed in with some Western Sandpipers, and by chance happened to notice a juvenile Little Blue Heron. Just after sunset as we were leaving, sure that we couldn't find any more species that day, 3 Horned Larks flew in right next to us to take a dust bath. Ended Big Day with 124 species.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers our traverse through the harbor and about one mile outside the harbor to the edge of the 100-fathom curve.

Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

Sea & Sage Audubon held the first post-Covid annual fall pelagic trip today, October 3, aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Captain Peter Heistand and leaders Jon Dunn, Bruce Aird, Tom Benson, Robert McNab, and Steve Morris. Due to the oil spill off Huntington Beach we had to modify our normal route and instead headed southwest out of the harbor to Crespi Knoll, north to Lausen Sea Mount, northeast to the 100-fathom curve off Laguna Beach, and the southeast along the 100-fathom curve back to Dana Point. We encountered a few patches of oil from the spill as we were approaching Laguna Beach but they were  in a relatively concentrated area and we passed through them quickly. We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: Calm, overcast, mild temps. We started on the golf course where we were quickly escorted off, then checked creek and lower section. We finally found a (restricted) birding agreement for covering this place. Exotics (annoyingly) persists, though (luckily) the species don't seem to have yet taken hold in ensenada. Very happy to finally encounter two true vagrants here on the same visit, plus quite a few very good birds that were not traditional vagrants!----Day notes: On this day, we encountered the most incredible wave of Eastern passerine vagrants I have personally ever experienced in Baja. The combination of overcast, light winds (the ideal weather for the Baja north coast but seemingly not farther south), and incredible reports from San Diego and offshore Baja had us all excited for the prospects of today--and it panned out! There were vagrants EVERYWHERE! Not only a great introduction to Baja for CWH and AWH, but started the motto of "I've never seen anything here" leading to a vagrant that held through the entire trip.

column51: Calm, overcast, mild temps. We started on the golf course where we were quickly escorted off, then checked creek and lower section. We finally found a (restricted) birding agreement for covering this place. Exotics (annoyingly) persists, though (luckily) the species don't seem to have yet taken hold in ensenada. Very happy to finally encounter two true vagrants here on the same visit, plus quite a few very good birds that were not traditional vagrants!----Day notes: On this day, we encountered the most incredible wave of Eastern passerine vagrants I have personally ever experienced in Baja. The combination of overcast, light winds (the ideal weather for the Baja north coast but seemingly not farther south), and incredible reports from San Diego and offshore Baja had us all excited for the prospects of today--and it panned out! There were vagrants EVERYWHERE! Not only a great introduction to Baja for CWH and AWH, but started the motto of "I've never seen anything here" leading to a vagrant that held through the entire trip.

Just as I was finishing my bird walk and reached the top of the hill by brightwater a small raptor flew at an extremely high rate of speed over my head from behind.  lt flew much faster and was bulkier than the Kestrels I usually see there, about the size of a scrubjay or pigeon with a falcons pointy wings, long tail with bold bands quite visible in flight.  Much smaller than a coopers hawk and none of the coloring of the kestrel, pale white superciliary stripe above its eye  and white throat. Chest looked streaked as it flew overhead but the only pics I have of it are with it looking sideways from behind.  Two photographers ventured into the fenced habitat and got epic pictures from the front as it perched there for awhile  (they came through from the trail below where the herons nest in the palms up to Brightwater).  They told me this snag is the merlin's favorite perch.  I have pictures of everything I noted today (for being such a white out crummy day,  most are fairly clear except for birds in flight)

I footpedaled up there to cover the 3.7 mile distance quicker so the tide would be still high and then paddled back to the bridge, then footpedaled home.  Very quiet back in the backbay with the most noise coming from the Forsters terns and canada geese.  Saw the Science center boat out in the bay- they said there were some baby Yellow Crowned Night Herons by the point past the science center- I didn't see them but saw two adult yellow crowned night herons about 200 yds before the  buoys marking the end of the allowed area. The white crown stripe was buffy-yellow at the forehead, There was a very small buffy-yellow chin patch under the lower mandible, otherwise the chin and throat were black. Uniformly gray-bodied with scapulars, back, and wing coverts having the appearance of being heavily streaked with black. There were some very long plumes on the back. I did not see any plumes on the head. Bill was straighter and thicker than on Black-crowned Night Heron. Eyes were orang-ish. Legs were long and yellow. Bird perched motionlessly in a mostly bare tree at the end of the chain-link fence across the small inlet from the sailing school.

Pelagic trip aboard the zodiac Skimmer with Capt Ryan. --From Newport harbor, we first went towards Lausen Sea Mount following large flocks of Black-vented Shearwaters. We turned south there, crossing over into LA county waters near Crespi knoll. We worked our way to the top of the 30-mile bank and followed the bank south to the San Diego county line, laying a couple of oil slicks on this stretch. At the SD county line, with the wind getting stronger, we turned northeast, joining the escarpment near San Onofre. From here, we followed the shelf all the way back in to Newport Harbor.--The day started of with very dense fog nearshore, clearing to a high cloud ceiling for much of the day until we returned back to some patchy fog nearshore on the way back. Seas were up to 3-4 ft. Winds were calm in the morning, picking up in the afternoon with plenty of whitecaps and some spray on the boat.--Marine mammals included Minke, Fin and Bryde's whales, long-beaked and short-beaked common dolphins, Risso's dolphins and bottlenose dolphins.--This leg from the dock to the harbor mouth in the densest fog I've ever seen here. Marking the list incomplete because of difficult birding conditions and we weren't paying full attention

column51: Pelagic trip aboard the zodiac Skimmer with Capt Ryan. --From Newport harbor, we first went towards Lausen Sea Mount following large flocks of Black-vented Shearwaters. We turned south there, crossing over into LA county waters near Crespi knoll. We worked our way to the top of the 30-mile bank and followed the bank south to the San Diego county line, laying a couple of oil slicks on this stretch. At the SD county line, with the wind getting stronger, we turned northeast, joining the escarpment near San Onofre. From here, we followed the shelf all the way back in to Newport Harbor.--The day started of with very dense fog nearshore, clearing to a high cloud ceiling for much of the day until we returned back to some patchy fog nearshore on the way back. Seas were up to 3-4 ft. Winds were calm in the morning, picking up in the afternoon with plenty of whitecaps and some spray on the boat.--Marine mammals included Minke, Fin and Bryde's whales, long-beaked and short-beaked common dolphins, Risso's dolphins and bottlenose dolphins.--This leg from the dock to the harbor mouth in the densest fog I've ever seen here. column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel northwest toward Catalina Island, from which we cut back east across the Lausen Sea Mount on our return to Dana Point. This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab, and our captain Brittany Loust on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:15 am, and left the dock at 7:18 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth and the breakwaters at 7:30 am to continue offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended about 1.6 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 26" N, 117° 41' 51" W). Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly and stopped only briefly, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. There was a full, low overcast throughout this period, calm conditions, and a temperature of 60° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle on his arrival). The waters just off the breakwater had a roughly one-foot swell from the west and a rippled surface. 7:15-7:35 am.----California Sea Lion - 12 (seen around the outer buoy just offshore).----The track for the day is shown below, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list, and the cyan pins showing the locations of the more interesting species seen. column51: I only birded the San Juan creek mouth. You have two options for parking/access: you can park in the eastern lot for doheney state beach($15 entry fee), or a longer walk(0.4 miles each way) park at Del obispo park walk behind ballfields get on bike path for creek here (33.4683429, -117.6823480) and walk to creek mouth for free. ----The gull flock can be anywhere-in the creek mouth of on the beach. If you’re here at low tide, the beach has an extended area of tide pool rocks that the gulls like during low tide. ----I left just now. Too dark to continue looking. I had a definite Franklin’s Gull in creek mouth. Multiple Glaucous- winged and Bonaparte’s. One Iceland(maybe more). A few herring. One first cycle Short-billed, lots of the expected common species. And then a possible first cycle Lesser-black Backed amongst the flock. I have more photos to review. I was unable to refind it when I lost it but it still is in the area and will likely be with the flock-but gulls at this location can be anywhere. I encourage others to expand the search area last the creek mouth if not having success or if the flock isn’t there-it’s always in the area on the beach. If not there either, then it’s likely in the harbor somewhere, on the jetties.----Gorgeous evening. Mostly sunny, nice breeze, mid 60s. Epic gulling. One way mileage from Del obispo community center parking lot.

We observed at least two adult individuals nesting in a tree off Appian Way, as well as one juvenile, at approximately 33.754754, -118.116801. Matched the visage of a confirmed vagrant juvenile YCNH that I observed at Seneca Lake in San Carlos, AZ on 5/11/22.  One poor pic of one of the adults, but its enough to see the head markings. column52: Juvenile on the pond. Second record for this pond. I was scanning the pond and came across a night heron, and was shocked to see that it very gray in color. I ran back to my car to get my scope, and then was able to confirm it was a Yellow-crowned. Compared to Black-crowned, the overall color was very different, being a silvery-gray compared to the brown of a Black-crowned. The bill was very thick and entirely dark. The chin was white. The head was dark and covered in small white spots. The wings were also covered in small white spots. Unfortunately there was no service here, so i drove to pescadero to let people know. Sadly, the bird was no longer present when I got back to the pond about 35 minutes later. However, I think the bird is still very likely in the area, and is likely foraging in the pond during the early morning and late afternoon.

column51: Field Trip with Conejo Audubon with Martin Ruane and David Pereksta leading. Arrived on a 6.6' high tide that was starting to fall, but the lagoon was still incredibly full. That combined with high winds coming down Calleguas Creek made it very difficult to scope the lagoon and the ocean at the onset of the trip. A potential Short-eared Owl perched up in the marsh could not be confirmed due to the distance and the wind rattling the scopes around. column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel northwest toward Catalina Island, from which we cut back east across the Lausen Sea Mount on our return to Dana Point. This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab, and our captain Brittany Loust on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:15 am, and left the dock at 7:18 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth and the breakwaters at 7:30 am to continue offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended about 1.6 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 26" N, 117° 41' 51" W). Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly and stopped only briefly, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. There was a full, low overcast throughout this period, calm conditions, and a temperature of 60° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle on his arrival). The waters just off the breakwater had a roughly one-foot swell from the west and a rippled surface. 7:15-7:35 am.----California Sea Lion - 12 (seen around the outer buoy just offshore).----The track for the day is shown below, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list, and the cyan pins showing the locations of the more interesting species seen. This report represents the last of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Peter Heistand as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  We ended our day by returning to the Dana Point Harbor, where we reached the Ocean Institute dock at 4:03 pm, after passing through the harbor mouth at 3:53 pm.  This list ends about the time we departed the boat.  Given that we passed relatively rapidly through the main harbor channel without stopping, and only superficially checking the breakwaters and the shore of island, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.95 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance for our trip through the inshore waters and the harbor.  On our return to port, there was a full, mid-level overcast, a mild (<5 knot) breeze from the west, and at the end of this period, a temperature of 72° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle).  The seas continued at about one foot with a rippled surface.  3:45-4:05 pm.----California Ground-Squirrel - 3 (calling; we heard and saw several ground-squirrels while we passed by the island in the middle of the harbor);--California Sea Lion - 4 (loafing together on a marker buoy just off the breakwater).

column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel northwest toward Catalina Island, from which we cut back east across the Lausen Sea Mount on our return to Dana Point. This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab, and our captain Brittany Loust on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:15 am, and left the dock at 7:18 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth and the breakwaters at 7:30 am to continue offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended about 1.6 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 26" N, 117° 41' 51" W). Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly and stopped only briefly, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. There was a full, low overcast throughout this period, calm conditions, and a temperature of 60° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle on his arrival). The waters just off the breakwater had a roughly one-foot swell from the west and a rippled surface. 7:15-7:35 am.----California Sea Lion - 12 (seen around the outer buoy just offshore).----The track for the day is shown below, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list, and the cyan pins showing the locations of the more interesting species seen. column52: RC: Presumably the same bird from last winter returning. It was last seen on March 31 when the BCNH left, it also left. We don’t know where these BCNH go to nest, but I had hoped it would come back with the flock. It was not here on November 7 when I brought my class.--DR writes: in my series of photos over 15 minutes, all of them showed the eyelid closed (as my second photo here), as if the bird was very tired. Last year the first MTY record was found in these same cypresses on 5 Dec 2023; it remained to 31 March 2024. Our discovery this year is 13 days earlier in the late fall season. In photos I compared the pattern of blackish and dull yellow on the lower mandible of today's bird and last December's photos. To me it appears to be a similar pattern: a dull yellow triangular wedge being broadest at the base. This does appear to be the same individual returning.--We don't know where it went for the summer, but Rick Fournier had an adult YCNH in the night-heron colony on the Packard Ranch, on Elkhorn Slough, on 25 Oct 2024. Although the photo is distant, I do see a similar pale wedge in Rick's photo. I reviewed the color pattern of adult YCNH photo in eBird across the southern U.S. There was a lot of variation: a fair percentage all black, some that looked like our PB bird, and others with varying shapes of whitish or yellow on the lower mandible. The fact that the Elkhorn Slough adult has a similarly shaped pale patch on lower mandible is some support to thinking it might be the same bird that is wintering in Pebble Beach again. The only other active breeding colony we know about in MTY is at Pt. Lobos. [Another colony at Zmudowski pond disappeared some years ago.]

column51: This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:05 am, and left the dock at 7:07 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:17 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 23" N, 117° 42' 04" W). We saw only moderate numbers of gulls and cormorants on the breakwater, but many pelicans. Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 2.59 miles, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we had a moderately dense fog that reached the water, calm conditions at the dock but a mild (5+ knot) breeze from the west just offshore, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were mild, with a 1-2 foot swell from the west and a rippled surface. 7:05-7:25 am.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. column51: This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:05 am, and left the dock at 7:07 am. Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. This report represents the last in a set of eight lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns. Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants. Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds. Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock. On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----
