column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our afternoon transit over the inshore waters between the escarpment and the harbor mouth and through the harbor back to the dock.

This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list. Its long neck folded in front. The latest checklist removes the hyphen from "Night-Heron." Typically hyphenated names indicate monophyletic groups while removing the hyphen indicates otherwise. In this case there are some more distantly related herons also called Night Herons, thus the hyphen was removed from all of them. The characteristic large swollen bill is specialized for eating crabs. They have expanded their range with multiple pairs breeding in coastal Southern California as far north as Ventura County. Their first successful California nesting was in 2006 at San Diego. This is the subspecies "N. v. bancrofti" characterized by paler coloration, narrower dorsal streaks and having a thicker bill than the nominate East Coast race.

This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns. Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants. Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds. Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock. On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----

We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns. Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants. Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds. Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock. On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----

This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. column52: RC: Presumably the same bird from last winter returning. We don’t know where these BCNH go to nest, but I had hoped it would come back with the flock. It was not here on November 7 when I brought my class. Photos--DR writes: in my series of photos over 15 minutes, all of them showed the eyelid closed (as my second photo here), as if the bird was very tired. Last year the first MTY record was found in these same cypresses on 5 Dec 2023; it remained to 31 March 2024. Our discovery this year is 12 days earlier in the late fall season. In photos I compared the pattern of blackish and dull yellow on the lower mandible of today's bird and last December's photos. To me it appears to be a similar pattern: a dull yellow triangular wedge being broadest at the base. This does appear to be the same individual returning.--   We don't know where it went for the summer, but Rick Fournier had an adult YCNH in the night-heron colony on the Packard Ranch, on Elkhorn Slough, on 25 Oct 2024. Although the photo is distant, I do see a similar pale wedge in Rick's photo. I reviewed the color pattern of adult YCNH photo in eBird across the southern U.S.  There was a lot of variation: a fair percentage all black, some that looked like our PB bird, and others with varying shapes of whitish or yellow on the lower mandible. The fact that the Elkhorn Slough adult has a similarly shaped pale patch on lower mandible is some support to thinking it might be the same bird that is wintering in Pebble Beach again. The only other active breeding colony we know about in MTY is at Pt. Lobos. [Another colony at Zmudowshi pond has disappeared some years ago.]

This report represents the last in a set of eight lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. column51: This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

column51: This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our morning transit through the harbor and the inshore waters between the harbor mouth and the escarpment.

column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns. Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants. Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds. Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock. On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----

This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our afternoon transit over the inshore waters between the escarpment and the harbor mouth and through the harbor back to the dock.

We visited the nearshore escarpment from the 279 Bank, Crespi Knoll, Lausen Sea Mount, and the nearshore escarpment between Laguna Beach and Dana Point during our 9-hour trip. There was a relatively low, complete cloud cover for the entire morning, with the clouds breaking just afternoon and giving way to clear skies for the last few hours of the trip. column51: This report represents the last in a set of eight lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list. We traveled along this path in a generally clockwise direction, albeit with a Figure-8 that took us in a counterclockwise loop over Crespi Knoll.----

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our morning transit through the harbor and the inshore waters between the harbor mouth and the escarpment.

This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our afternoon transit over the inshore waters between the escarpment and the harbor mouth and through the harbor back to the dock.

This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). column51: This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W). We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer. We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow. Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore. On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). column51: This report represents the last in a set of eight lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list. column51: This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

column51: Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (<10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our afternoon transit over the inshore waters between the escarpment and the harbor mouth and through the harbor back to the dock.

column51: This report represents the last in a set of eight lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm. We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans. We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle). The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface. Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list.
