This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock. We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm. This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout. We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants. We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether. Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds. Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe. Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present. The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor. It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data). 3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----

column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

We departed the dock at the Ocean Institute in Dana Point Harbor a little after 7:00 AM, and upon exiting the harbor traveled southwest toward the north end of Crespi Knoll, with a few deviations to check out birds. We traveled a U-shaped, clockwise path around Crespi Knoll, then headed northwest over the Catalina Ridge southeast of Catalina Island. Upon reaching our allotted time limit, we then traveled east back to Dana Point Harbor, arriving at the dock a little before 4:00 PM. The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. This list covers our afternoon traverse from the edge of the 100-fathom curve to the jetty and through the harbor.

column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

column52: Two juvenile birds near the landing cove.  In the field I assumed Black-crowned but on photo review the structure of the bird was a bit off for Black-crowned. Initially had difficulty discerning which species I was looking at when I reviewed pictures. They were showing small triangular spots on the back and wings with thin white lines but to me this was not the best field mark but was a contributing factor. The spots were sharper looking than the blurry triangular spots on Black-crowned. These birds on Anacapa have a heavier looking bill and more blunt tip than expected on Black-crowned which is also rare for this location. Consulted more experience birders and they confirmed Yellow-crowned Night Heron.  At least one of the birds was standing tall and seemed to have long legs, and a thinner body with a more blocky head. To me Black-crowned seem stockier with a more rounded head into a thicker neck.

column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

We spent several hours scanning the ponds and bays, carefully scrutinizing the masses of terns flying over and perched along the edges of Pond 12 to no avail. Justyn left around 9:30, and Jimmy bailed out at 10:30. We walked up to check Pond 15, but then continued staking out Pond 12 after that, eventually being joined by Robert Patton and Elizabeth Copper. At about 1pm, Matt was scoping the end of the Chula Vista jetty when he spotted an interesting bird; his views were brief and very distant, but suggestive enough that we decided to end our vigil and check out the jetty. Conditions were generally good: overcast till about 11, then the marine layer slowly started to break up; temps in the mid 60s to mid 70s, a bit of a breeze picked up once the clouds started to disperse.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

This list covers our morning traverse through the harbor and out to the edge of the 100-fathom curve.

column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

column51: The long version: Jill had just arrived before me, not sure about Jason and Edana but we all were actively looking for the heron near Lam-son’s coordinates and had located a distant motley crew of YCNHs and unknowns when about 5 minutes in Jill noted some hint of tell-tale white on the heron that was spread out from the main grouping. It appeared to be coming back online and started to peek out from the tall grass at the edge of the even higher spiny rush tussocks along the road north of the bridge. The white in the throat was apparent and more so was the reddish (for me at least) from the bridge with my lens at about 700mm. It seemed to be rousing and then took flight quickly landing across the water to the north by the elbow in the path before it bends to go parallel with the road. Birders managed flight shots which could have worked for ID but I took off running (lol I’m sure it was comical to watch), having only a few minutes remaining before I had to depart. Jill and Jason too, we all huffed over to the inner walkway but could not relocate the bird. I had already checked the left waterway (north side) from the path to no avail. Then tried the original south side. Nothing. Then again on the north side— it emerged! I hollered to Jill and Jason who were facing south and they came over and we collectively rejoiced. Bird was lost again as I was leaving, I hustled away but soon I became adjacent to the opening of the mini side ravine on rabbit island halfway along the perpendicular path and I saw the heron working the stream there just as Edana arrived from the opposite direction. Cooler looks/pics from that spot for sure. Can you tell I’m excited? Sorry for the lengthy journal entry. I’m still new to this so — still naive and over-explaining yay.

column51: Pasadena Audubon Society sponsored a 9-hour pelagic trip out of Dana Point aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Peter Heistand as captain, and Luke Tiller, Jon Feenstra, Matt Brady, Brittany O'Connor, and Tom Benson as co-leaders. We departed the dock at the Ocean Institute in Dana Point Harbor a little after 7:00 AM, and upon exiting the harbor traveled southwest toward the north end of Crespi Knoll, with a few deviations to check out birds. We traveled a U-shaped, clockwise path around Crespi Knoll, then headed northwest over the Catalina Ridge southeast of Catalina Island. Upon reaching our allotted time limit, we then traveled east back to Dana Point Harbor, arriving at the dock a little before 4:00 PM. The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. This list covers our morning traverse through the harbor and out to the edge of the 100-fathom curve.

column52: Continuing rarity re-found a few days ago by Kelli O'Neill, back for its third known season at the north Natomas heron and egret rookery. When I arrived the bird was resting, making very little movements on a horizontal branch near the top of the Eastmost willow on the West Island. Its eyes were closed and its long neck was tucked in. I could see the all black head interrupted by a white cheek patch that is widest and circular at the back of the cheek but narrows to a point at the front. Medium sized gray bill. The forehead of the bird is a rich daisy yellow color. The body of the bird is all smooth gray with black triangular streaks on the back. The legs are bright pink. I noticed a collection of twigs by its feet. --Detailed notes about its behavior: --About around 11 am, the bird awoke, lifted its long neck, and I could see its reddish orange eye. The six or seven long and thin white plume feathers on the back of its head raised to be almost completely vertical. The bird began to display, all of its feathers fluffed up, making the bird bigger. Its extraordinary long slender back plumes raised. The bird then opened its wings and bowed, the bottom of its neck lowering the farthest, its lower back lifting. Then the bird returned to its normal posture. It displayed to no noticeable bird a few times, then a Black Crowned Night Heron flew on its branch in front of it. The YCNH changed positions and displayed facing the BCNH (and also facing me). From the front the bird's display is gorgeous, its raised spidery back plumes create the illusion that the bird is wearing a giant Mohawk. The YCNH displayed once for the BCNH, and then the BCNH flew off. The YCNH began climbing down from its perch, and displayed for other BCNH perched lower in the willow. None of them indicated interest. The YCNH then flew down to the bottom of the island, and walked towards the trunk of a Sycamore. It then picked up a longish twig below the tree. It kept setting it down and picking it back up, before leaving it entirely. The heron began to walk back towards the base of the willow, but was spooked by a sitting Canada Goose that struck its elongated neck toward it with its bill open. The heron hopped backwards in response and began walking north of the willow, and disappeared down the back slope of the island. It re-appeared up the slope with another twig in its bill, and flew back to its spot in the willow. The bird then lowered the twig into the pile by its feet and shuffled it into the pile, shaking its head slightly, perhaps to help weave the stick into the makeshift nest. The bird also maneuvered different twigs around to perhaps make the new one fit better. After it was done, it displayed a few more times with its back to me, then resumed resting in place. I did not get pictures.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

We departed the dock at the Ocean Institute in Dana Point Harbor a little after 7:00 AM, and upon exiting the harbor traveled southwest toward the north end of Crespi Knoll, with a few deviations to check out birds. We traveled a U-shaped, clockwise path around Crespi Knoll, then headed northwest over the Catalina Ridge southeast of Catalina Island. Upon reaching our allotted time limit, we then traveled east back to Dana Point Harbor, arriving at the dock a little before 4:00 PM. The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. This list covers our afternoon traverse from the edge of the 100-fathom curve to the jetty and through the harbor.

column51: I chased the continuing Bar-tailed Godwit, which involved walking up to the crowd of people, looking in Curtis’s scope to see the bird, then staring at it as it mostly slept for about an hour. Eventually it started to become more active as the flock of Willets and Whimbrels it was associating with flew off from the main flock in small groups. Finally, it flew across the channel and settled in to continue snoozing. At this point I walked down to the bridge, crossed to the north side of the channel, and walked back up the channel to where the bird was sleeping, where I had great views. A bunch of other people were present for some or all of my stay, including Curtis, Naresh, the Scheels, TFH, and others whom I did not know. After watching it here for a further fifteen minutes or so, my parking pass was about to expire, so I left. Conditions were nice: highish tide, clear skies, warm in the high 70s, light onshore breeze. Tons of people around but the birds didnt seem to care much.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. column51: This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

column51: This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a <5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.

column51: Pasadena Audubon Society sponsored a 9-hour pelagic trip out of Dana Point aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Peter Heistand as captain, and Luke Tiller, Jon Feenstra, Matt Brady, Brittany O'Connor, and Tom Benson as co-leaders. We departed the dock at the Ocean Institute in Dana Point Harbor a little after 7:00 AM, and upon exiting the harbor traveled southwest toward the north end of Crespi Knoll, with a few deviations to check out birds. We traveled a U-shaped, clockwise path around Crespi Knoll, then headed northwest over the Catalina Ridge southeast of Catalina Island. Upon reaching our allotted time limit, we then traveled east back to Dana Point Harbor, arriving at the dock a little before 4:00 PM. The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. This list covers our afternoon traverse from the edge of the 100-fathom curve to the jetty and through the harbor.

column51: Pasadena Audubon Society sponsored a 9-hour pelagic trip out of Dana Point aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Peter Heistand as captain, and Luke Tiller, Jon Feenstra, Matt Brady, Brittany O'Connor, and Tom Benson as co-leaders. We departed the dock at the Ocean Institute in Dana Point Harbor a little after 7:00 AM, and upon exiting the harbor traveled southwest toward the north end of Crespi Knoll, with a few deviations to check out birds. We traveled a U-shaped, clockwise path around Crespi Knoll, then headed northwest over the Catalina Ridge southeast of Catalina Island. Upon reaching our allotted time limit, we then traveled east back to Dana Point Harbor, arriving at the dock a little before 4:00 PM. The morning started out with a relatively high marine layer (100% cloud cover) that started to break up mid day, with partly cloudy skies in the afternoon. Temperatures ranged from the upper 60s to low 70s, with variable winds up to 13 mph. There was a 3-5' swell from the south with an average wave period of 10 seconds for most of the day. This list covers our morning traverse through the harbor and out to the edge of the 100-fathom curve.

Jason was there when I arrived and then Jennifer arrived. We spotted the tri colored heron hunkered down and very hard to see back beyond the pickle weed by the native shrubs closer to PCH than the walkbridge but not visible from the trail that parallels PCH. (observed from the walkbridge on the left or Warner street side of the bridge as opposed to Seapoint). A scope would be most helpful if it were in this concealed spot. It was in the same area with at least 3 yellow crown night herons (two juveniles and one adult) . Edana arrived and we observed the bird pop out and fly across to the PCH side of the innerbay trail maybe 100 yards below the observation point. Jason, Jennifer and I sprinted over there to see if we could get some pics. Jennifer respotted the bird as it had flown to the inland side of the innerbay trail. We observed it walk along the sandbar at the water's edge before it disappeared in the pickle weed. It reappeared about 40 feet down minutes later in a little gully. It walked along the sandbar foraging for maybe 4-5 minutes then abruptly flew across the innerbay trail to the other side. It then foraged a few minutes longer and then flew back to the same spot Lam Son saw it in earlier by the walkbridge. column52: Observed a medium-sized, stocky heron resting on a fallen log at the edge of still water, showing a compact build with a short thick neck, relatively short legs, and crisp gray plumage marked by fine vertical barring across the wings and back; the head pattern was diagnostic, with a solid black face, bright white cheek patch, pale yellowish crown stripe, orange eyes, and a thick dark bill. The bird held a typical night-heron posture, remaining mostly motionless in shaded, overgrown freshwater habitat. Identification as Yellow-crowned Night-Heron was based on the distinctive head pattern, barred upperparts, and overall structure; Black-crowned Night-Heron was ruled out due to its smooth gray back, fully black cap, and different facial contrast, none of which matched the individual observed.

column51: This report represents one in a set of seven lists for the spring pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute and passed slowly through the main harbor channel. Upon exiting the harbor, we traveled generally southwest, crossing over the southeast corner of the 279 Bank on our way to the north end of Crespi Knoll, where we laid out a chum slick and watched for an hour as storm-petrels visited the slick. We then made a clockwise traverse around the perimeter of the knoll, returning to the site of our chum slick before returning to Dana Point by way of the 279 Bank. ----Weather conditions started at a full, low-level overcast and remained that way for most of the morning, and mostly cloudy until we returned to the dock. A mild breeze persisted throughout most of the day, and temperatures ranged from the 50s to 60s (°F). Sea conditions throughout the day were generally calm.----This list began when the boat departed the dock and ended as we reached the close edge of the 100-fathom curve short distance offshore, not quite two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater.

column52: As I was driving by, I saw one adult yellow-crowned night heron fly across the road and into a Ficus tree. It immediately caught my attention because I had never observed a nesting yellow-crowned night heron in this area, though I knew from previous eBird reports that they nested in the area (https://ebird.org/atlascalifornia/checklist/S344242308). I stopped to investigate and observed an adult feeding an immature bird, which I photographed. The adult then departed, leaving the young bird in the nest.----From my vantage point, I could only see one juvenile, and I did not have my binoculars or camera with me to get a better view into the canopy. While looking through the tree, I also noticed at least 15 other unoccupied nests, which may have been a mix of BCNH and YCNH.

Shores Park) to the West Mission Bay Drive bridge; Habitat: Coastal Salt Marsh & Tidal Mud Flat; Weather at start: 56 degrees F, overcast, wind: 3 mph ESE Weather at end: 64 degrees; partly cloudy; Tides: nearest high tide 6:19 am of 5.4 ft., nearest low tide 1:42 pm of -0.5 ft.  Elevation: 6 ft; Topography is flat; other species seen: California Ground Squirrel & Desert Cottontail; General Impressions & Highlights: students were mostly scattered as they focused their behavioral observations on specific species, Nick, Allie, and myself kept a list; birds were fairly active today, but tide was mostly high throughout with little mudflat so we mostly saw waterfowl; it had rained pretty well on Wednesday so might have contributed to water depth. However, we did have some shorebirds at the end of the trip, near the mission bay drive bridge. A surprise was three Yellow-Crowned Night Herons which flew north over the river and towards Sea World; a personal highlight was a group of about a dozen cormorants and 7 mergansers fishing and egrets following them, nabbing fish near the north shore, then towards mudflat and some emergent vegetation in the middle of the river, and then the egrets moved to the south side of the river and the mergansers and cormorants moved in that direction. Very active birds seemed to be driving the fish into these directions and the different species seemed to be cooperating. The burrowing owl seen on the previous two trips was back at its usual spot.

column51: Observer Jeff Boyd, entered into eBird by Naresh Satyan----Start Time: 5:45 am Stop Time: 10:30 am----Tide and Weather Conditions: Low tide was a negative 0.1 ft at 5:48 am; while I was checking for shorebirds south of Anaheim St, the tide was rising between plus 0.6.and 3.0 ft and was good for shorebirds, especially on my way downriver.----The sky was clear then partly cloudy overnight, and there were patchy clouds from dawn until about 7:30 am followed by complete clearing through duration of count.----The temperature ranged from 69 degrees at start time to 80 degrees at stop time. There was no breeze until after 10:00 am and was then about 5mph from the south.----Additional Comments: Today's count of 33 Black Oystercatchers was my highest ever for the lower river but was in keeping with my totals for this species in the upper 20s throughout June. There were significantly lower numbers today for a few fish-eating species, in particular Brown Pelican and Elegant Tern. Following the Boyle Heights warehouse fire this June, there'd been a die-off of green algae followed closely by a significant fish die-off. The algae has made a quick comeback, and the fish are beginning to repopulate the lower river but not yet in such numbers as to support the numbers of fish-eating birds that we usually have on the river at this time of year.

We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute and passed slowly through the main harbor channel.  Upon exiting the harbor, we traveled generally southwest, crossing over the southeast corner of the 279 Bank on our way to the north end of Crespi Knoll, where we made a clockwise, u-shaped traverse around the perimeter of the knoll. We then continued north to Lausen Sea Mount, navigating over the high point and then travelling northeast toward Newport Canyons. Upon reaching the 100-fathom Curve, we followed it southeast back to Dana Point.----Weather conditions started at a nearly full, mid-level overcast, becoming mostly cloudy by mid-morning and mostly sunny and clear by about noon, with 5-15% cloud cover until we returned to the dock. A mild (5 knot) breeze from the west persisted throughout most of the day, and temperatures ranged from about 58-64° F. Sea conditions throughout the day were generally calm, with a wave height of 2-3 feet from the southwest and sea temperatures approximately 59-62° F.----This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, not quite two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater. ----Bottlenose Dolphin - 1

This report represents one in a set of ten lists for the winter, pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute and passed slowly through the main harbor channel.  Upon exiting the harbor, we traveled generally southwest, crossing over the southeast corner of the 279 Bank on our way to the north end of Crespi Knoll, where we made a clockwise, u-shaped traverse around the perimeter of the knoll. We then continued north to Lausen Sea Mount, navigating over the high point and then travelling northeast toward Newport Canyons. Upon reaching the 100-fathom Curve, we followed it southeast back to Dana Point.----Weather conditions started at a nearly full, mid-level overcast, becoming mostly cloudy by mid-morning and mostly sunny and clear by about noon, with 5-15% cloud cover until we returned to the dock. A mild (5 knot) breeze from the west persisted throughout most of the day, and temperatures ranged from about 58-64° F. Sea conditions throughout the day were generally calm, with a wave height of 2-3 feet from the southwest and sea temperatures approximately 59-62° F.----This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, not quite two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater. ----Bottlenose Dolphin - 1

column51: This report represents one in a set of ten lists for the winter, pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute and passed slowly through the main harbor channel.  Upon exiting the harbor, we traveled generally southwest, crossing over the southeast corner of the 279 Bank on our way to the north end of Crespi Knoll, where we made a clockwise, u-shaped traverse around the perimeter of the knoll. We then continued north to Lausen Sea Mount, navigating over the high point and then travelling northeast toward Newport Canyons. Upon reaching the 100-fathom Curve, we followed it southeast back to Dana Point.----Weather conditions started at a nearly full, mid-level overcast, becoming mostly cloudy by mid-morning and mostly sunny and clear by about noon, with 5-15% cloud cover until we returned to the dock. A mild (5 knot) breeze from the west persisted throughout most of the day, and temperatures ranged from about 58-64° F. Sea conditions throughout the day were generally calm, with a wave height of 2-3 feet from the southwest and sea temperatures approximately 59-62° F.----This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, not quite two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater. ----Bottlenose Dolphin - 1

Clear; warm; light breeze.--After burning up a lot of time earlier today on two unsuccessful wild warbler chases, we were in a rush to see if we could locate the lingering juvenile LBHE at Bolsa Chica. Our first attempt was to park on the shoulder of the highway opposite the dam, where there was a cluster of white egrets. Very exposed, a bit dangerous. Dick remained in the car. I hopped out, scanned the egrets, found no Little Blue, and rushed back to the car. We whipped around, parked in the parking lot at the boardwalk, and were prepared to hoof it deeper into the lagoon. Instead, the heron was right. there. we spent a few minutes admiring it, then returned to the car, and headed off in search of our (my) next tick.--I try to aim for complete checklists, but there's no way to pretend that, with all that commotion and the brevity of our visit, we were capable of compiling a complete checklist, so am submitting this as Incomplete. Dirty twitching, that's all this is. 70-73 degrees, 60% cloud cover, 5-8 wind. Mostly stationary scoping from 32.61889, -117.1033, incomplete list. Chase trip for Siberian Sand-Plover. Yesterday, I attempted to chase, but the plover departed about 30 minutes before I would arrive, so I turned around. When I arrived today, the plover was not in view, last seen vanishing behind an oyster ball berm. My luck began to turn positive when Sylvia, Omar and Finn arrived. HUGE sigh of relief when Omar relocated the plover (only a few of us left to look with 2 scopes) around 1:15ish, near the tall bluish-brown pole embedded in the mudflats (vs. poles in the water). We observed the plover for approx. 5-10 minutes, before the bird disappeared again. We stuck around for another hour-plus, hoping to see the plover again, but eventually decided to throw in the towel. Thankfully, Matt relocated the bird just before we left the area. We drove back to the parking lot and began scoping where we saw Matt's car - a muddy spit area east of the dark "cliff." Life bird. As Curtis would say, "better views desired." Thank goodness the plover was in alternate plumage (the orange chest really stood out) - otherwise it would be hopeless. Added to my negative-star rated photo collection :)
